We assessed implicit and explicit measures of six types of discrimination-racism, sexism, heterosexism, cissexism, ageism, and sizeism-and used regression-based modeling to assess crude and adjusted associations of measures with sleep outcomes. We found that target groups generally reported shorter sleep duration and worse sleep disturbance and impairment than dominant groups, though only shorter sleep duration among People of Color remained significant in adjusted models. Associations between implicit and explicit measures and sleep outcomes were largely attenuated after adjustment, though independent effects emerged for sexism among women in relation to sleep impairment. Findings highlight the complex relationships of recognition of discrimination and implicit preferences with sleep health and the importance of multidimensional approaches to measuring discrimination. Future longitudinal and larger sample population studies are needed to clarify mechanisms, consider intersectional identities and experiences, and identify intervention targets to advance sleep equity and population health. Our findings highlight the necessity of funding rigorous research on discrimination and health; defunding such research undermines scientific integrity, public health, and the goal of ensuring that all populations can thrive.

papers.title: Piezoelectric actuator-evoked mechano-gated currents in trigeminal neurons innervating the mouse temporomandibular joint.
papers.abstract: The most burdensome symptom of temporomandibular joint disorders (TMJDs) is mechanically evoked pain. To identify the trigeminal ganglion (TG) neuronal subtypes mediating mechanical sensitivity, we combined whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology with immunohistochemistry (IHC) to characterize mouse TMJ-innervating TG neurons retrogradely labeled from the TMJ. Electrophysiological analysis identified five distinct neuronal groups, only one of which responded to piezo actuator-induced mechanical stimulation. TMJ innervation was dominated by C- and A-nociceptors, comprising four of the five identified groups. The fifth, a minor population of small-diameter neurons (S1), displayed properties consistent with either vGlut3-positive, C-low-threshold mechanoreceptors (C-LTMRs) or Sst-positive neurons. Two mechanically insensitive C-nociceptor groups, distinguished by their action potential firing patterns, likely corresponded to CGRP-positive and non-Mrgpr neuronal populations. One mechanically insensitive A-nociceptor group likely represented Smr2-positive Aδ high-threshold mechanoreceptors (Aδ-HTMRs). The only mechanically responsive neurons were large-diameter A-nociceptors, which likely correspond to the weakly TrkC- expressing neuronal population. No recorded neurons displayed electrophysiological characteristics of classical A-LTMRs. Together, these findings demonstrate that the TMJ is innervated by a distinct repertoire of TG sensory neurons compared with the skin and masseter muscle, with mechanically responsive afferents restricted to a single A-nociceptor subtype rather than classical low-threshold mechanoreceptors.

papers.title: Reviewer Comment on Patrick et al. "Evaluating EEG Requisition Quality and Clinical Factors Influencing Outcomes: A Retrospective Audit".
papers.journal: The Canadian journal of neurological sciences. Le journal canadien des sciences neurologiques

papers.title: A First Case of Compulsive Amnestic Sleep-Related Shopping Induced by Pramipexole Therapy of Restless Legs Syndrome.
papers.abstract: Dopamine receptor agonists (DAs) such as pramipexole/ropinirole are recognized treatments for restless legs syndrome (RLS) and Parkinson's disease (PD). It is well established that these medications can cause impulse control disorders (ICDs) during wakefulness, side effects with serious and potentially life-altering consequences. Impulse control disorders are recurrent difficult-to-resist behaviors that can be harmful to the patient or others around them. Common examples include pathologic gambling and compulsive sexual behaviors, eating, and shopping. We present the case of a patient with RLS who developed pathologic nocturnal sleep-related shopping, without recalling the events, which resolved after discontinuing pramipexole. This case illustrates the devastating consequences that unrecognized medically-induced ICDs can have on patients' lives and the importance of counseling patients about ICDs during wake and sleep prior to starting DA therapy.

papers.title: Diaphragm 'atonia' during ictal and post-ictal apnoea: A case report.
papers.abstract: Ictal and post ictal central apnoea (ICA and PCA) are driven by suppression of brainstem respiratory drive and represent an electroclinical biomarker of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). While animal models have demonstrated a true 'atonic diaphragm' underlying seizure-related apnoea, no human polygraphic study has yet confirmed respiratory muscle 'atonia' with direct EMG recording. In this case report, we present a 26-year-old female with meningoencephalocele-associated temporal lobe epilepsy who underwent a video-EEG polygraphy integrated with surface EMG from intercostals muscles and the diaphragm. We recorded a left frontotemporal seizure with ICA and four consecutives PCA events, all accompanied by surface electromyographic silence of the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles. This case provide a human polygraphic evidence of diaphragm and intercostal muscles silence during ICA and PCA, confirming the cascade of respiratory inhibition through brainstem respiratory centres down to respiratory muscles themselves. Notably, muscles relaxation occurred despite the patient was awake and able to follow commands. These findings support the importance of cardiorespiratory polygraphy during presurgical video-EEG evaluation, especially for temporal lobe seizures, to identify patients at higher SUDEP risk.

papers.title: Frontal Asymmetry in Infancy: Predictive Utility for Distinct Patterns of Temperament.
papers.abstract: Recent theorizing has emphasized motivational systems, rather than specific emotional reactions, when interpreting frontal asymmetry. We examined the predictive utility of infant electroencephalogram (EEG) frontal asymmetry during two approach-oriented tasks within 82 mother-infant dyads (infant age: M = 38.88 weeks, SD = 8.13 weeks; infant ethnicity: 86.7% Caucasian; infant sex: 51.2% female). Peek-a-Boo (PAB) and Toy Removal (TR) were chosen as predictors of mother-reported temperament, as both elicit approach motivation via a blocked goal in a joyful and frustrating context, respectively. TR asymmetry effect on Surgency/Positive Affectivity (SPA) was observed and driven primarily by a significant predictive relationship between TR asymmetry and Smiling and Laughter, f2 = 0.31. Negative Emotionality (NE) related outcomes were predicted by TR asymmetry, driven by Sadness, f2 = 0.20. Other than occasional contributions of covariates, no additional statistically significant results were noted. These findings are discussed as most consistent with the capability model of lateralization.

papers.title: Drosophila Appl loss disrupts proteins in mitochondrial oxidative and glycosylation pathways conserved in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: The physiological functions of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) remain unclear due to genetic redundancy and complex phenotypes. For decades, Drosophila amyloid precursor protein-like (Appl) research has relied on Appl d, a presumed null allele generated by irradiation. Here, we show that Appl d contains complex chromosomal rearrangements and background mutations confounding the interpretation of gene function. To address this, we created a precise CRISPR toolkit, including a clean null and a reporter allele. Deep proteomic profiling reveals that true Appl loss affects proteins associated with N-linked glycosylation, mitochondrial, and metabolic functions in a distinct signature from the background of Appl d. This conserved metabolic signature mirrors alterations in human patients and mouse Alzheimer's models and is associated with disrupted sleep and locomotion in flies. Our findings correct the genetic understanding of Appl, establishing it as a conserved regulator of metabolic balance essential for neuronal function.

papers.title: A 6-8-Hour Nighttime Sleep Strategy and Subsequent Cognitive Performance: A Target Trial Emulation Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep duration is a modifiable factor linked to cognitive aging among middle-aged and older adults, but existing evidence is largely correlational. Using observational data in which sleep duration was self-reported, we emulated a target trial to estimate the effect of maintaining a 6-8 h nighttime sleep strategy on subsequent cognitive performance. This target trial emulation study analyzed participants from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), a longitudinal, nationally representative prospective cohort of Chinese adults aged 45 years and older, and followed them from 2011 to 2020. Nocturnal sleep duration was self-reported at every wave. The 6-8 h sleep strategy was compared with a non-6-8 h strategy (<6h or >8h) using intention-to-treat (ITT), per-protocol (PP), and inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW)-weighted PP analyses. Primary outcome was the total cognitive score (range 0-21) after 9 years. Groups were balanced by 1:1 propensity-score matching (PSM) on 18 baseline covariates, and missing baseline covariate data were handled by multiple imputation by chained equations. Of 8147 eligible participants, 2341 matched pairs were included after PSM. The 6-8 h sleep strategy was consistently associated with higher cognitive scores than the non-6-8 h strategy in the ITT analysis (β = 0.237, 95% CI 0.016 to 0.458, p=0.036), the unweighted PP analysis (β = 0.394, 95% CI -0.013 to 0.801, p=0.058), and the IPCW-weighted PP analysis (β = 0.614, 95% CI 0.176 to 1.052, p=0.006). All estimates were modest in absolute terms, corresponding to 5.3% and 13.7% of one standard deviation of the outcome for the ITT and weighted PP analyses. The dose-response curve showed a nonlinear, inverted U-shaped association (P for non-linearity <0.001), with the highest predicted cognition at about 6.7 h of sleep. Neither sex nor age modified the association (P for interaction 0.84 and 0.27). By emulating a target trial with repeated prospective cohort data, this study moves beyond simple association and suggests that maintaining 6-8 h of self-reported nighttime sleep is associated with modestly higher subsequent cognitive performance. Target trial emulation improves the rigour of effect estimation but does not eliminate residual confounding, exposure misclassification or selective attrition; the findings require confirmation in studies using objective sleep assessment and more complete control of time-varying confounding.

papers.title: Impact of motor guided imagery therapy on stroke patients with pain symptoms: a three-level meta-analysis and systematic review of randomized controlled trials.
papers.abstract: Post-stroke pain is a common and intractable complication that hinders neurorehabilitation progress. Motor Guided Imagery (MGI), an emerging rehabilitation technique based on brain-computer interaction principles, has shown potential in relieving post-stroke pain, yet high-quality evidence on its multi-dimensional efficacy remains insufficient. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the effects of MGI on pain, sensorimotor function, sleep quality, life status, and psychological mood in stroke patients using a three-level meta-analysis. This study aimed to quantitatively assess the therapeutic effects of Motor Guided Imagery for stroke-related pain and explore potential intervention moderators using a three-level meta-analysis framework. Eight Chinese and English databases were searched from inception to June 29, 2025, to collect randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of MGI for stroke patients with pain. A three-level random-effects model was adopted to pool Hedges' g effect sizes, accompanied by heterogeneity testing, moderator analysis, influence analysis, and publication bias assessment. Influence-based outlier detection was implemented; analyses retaining all effect-size observations were treated as the primary main analysis, while outlier-removed analyses were reported only as supplementary sensitivity checks. Motor-guided imagery training significantly relieved pain (g = -0.524, 95% CI -0.779 to -0.269, p = 0.0006; negative Hedges' g indicates clinical improvement for this outcome) and improved sleep quality (g = -1.658, 95% CI -2.115 to -1.201, p < 0.001; negative Hedges' g indicates clinical improvement for this outcome) in stroke patients. Meanwhile, it significantly enhanced motor function (g = 1.395, 95% CI 0.963 to 1.826, p < 0.001), life status (g = 1.757, 95% CI 0.966 to 2.549, p = 0.0012), and psychological-emotional status (g = 1.729, 95% CI 1.045 to 2.413, p = 0.0002); positive Hedges' g indicates clinical improvement for the latter three outcomes. Moderator analysis indicated that acute-phase intervention (≤4 weeks) and high-frequency regimens (>5 sessions/week) tended to produce better analgesic effects, while age, gender, single-session duration, and pain location had no significant moderating effects. MGI may produce beneficial rehabilitation effects that can alleviate post-stroke pain and synergistically improve motor function, sleep, daily-living ability, and psychological state of stroke patients. Exploratory subgroup trends indicated potentially larger effects for early implementation within the acute phase and high-frequency short-duration regimens. However, these observations should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating clues given non-significant overall moderator tests. Further high-quality research is required to confirm these findings. The systematic review protocol was retrospectively registered with PROSPERO under registration ID CRD420261278812, after literature search and full-text screening had been completed. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261278812; identifier: CRD420261278812.

papers.title: Context-specific hypermetabolism in humans with mitochondrial defects.
papers.abstract: Pathogenic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) defects test how impaired oxidative phosphorylation reshapes human energy expenditure. We studied adults with confirmed mtDNA defects (MitoD) and healthy controls using whole-room indirect calorimetry, doubly labeled water, quantitative magnetic resonance, actigraphy, autonomic monitoring, mood assessments, plasma inflammatory markers, and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15). Under behaviorally clamped conditions, fat-free mass-adjusted 24-h energy expenditure (24-h EE) was consistently higher in MitoD, with higher non-resting expenditure per unit wrist acceleration by day, and blunted sleep-related metabolic suppression at night. In contrast, free-living total daily energy expenditure (TDEE) was similar between groups despite lower physical activity in MitoD, consistent with behavioral compensation within a constrained energy budget. Plasma GDF15 was ~5-fold higher in MitoD and tracked with disease severity, systemic inflammation, fatigue, energetic burden, and lower habitual activity. These findings identify a persistent energetic burden in MitoD that is buffered in daily life and associated with elevated GDF15.

papers.title: Relative Brain Perfusion Differences and Cognitive Improvement During Multimodal Management in a Patient With Progressive Cognitive Symptoms: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Progressive cognitive symptoms in older adults may reflect multiple interacting neurologic, vascular, sleep-related, medical, and lifestyle factors, making both etiologic attribution and assessment of treatment response challenging. We report the case of a 72-year-old man with approximately five years of progressive cognitive symptoms, including short-term memory impairment, slowed processing, distractibility, reduced initiative, and executive difficulties, in the setting of a remote cardiac arrest, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular risk, subsequent head trauma, and suspected sleep-disordered breathing. Baseline evaluation included a Self-Administered Gerocognitive Examination (SAGE) score of 9/22, minimal depressive symptoms, continuous performance testing, and adjunctive resting and concentration brain perfusion single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT). The SPECT findings were interpreted qualitatively as differences in relative regional tracer distribution and were not considered independently diagnostic. An individualized multimodal management plan emphasized sleep and circadian regularity, Mediterranean-style dietary measures, hydration, gradual aerobic and resistance exercise, cognitive and social engagement, and nonprescription nutritional supplementation without psychotropic medication. Over approximately six months, the patient and his wife reported improvement in memory, attention, organization, communication, motivation, and overall cognitive clarity, accompanied by renewed reading and cycling activity. Repeat SAGE increased by 9 points, from 9/22 to 18/22. Because several interventions were implemented concurrently, no single treatment component can be assigned a causal effect, and spontaneous improvement, natural variability, regression toward the mean, and practice effects cannot be excluded as contributors to the observed change. This case suggests that meaningful cognitive improvement may occur during individualized, multimodal longitudinal care while underscoring the importance of repeated reassessment and cautious interpretation of adjunctive brain perfusion SPECT.
keywords: brain perfusion single-photon emission computed tomography (spect)

papers.title: Why Sleep Matters in COPD: Cluster-Derived Sleep Phenotypes Reveal Distinct Physiological, Comorbidity and Survival Profiles.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are highly prevalent in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) but are not incorporated into current phenotypic classifications. We examined whether multidimensional sleep data identify clinically relevant patterns in COPD and whether these patterns are associated with all-cause mortality. In a clinical cohort of 205 patients with COPD, home-based sleep assessment was performed using the WatchPAT™ device. Fifteen complementary variables reflecting sleep duration and architecture, nocturnal oxygenation, sleep-disordered breathing, and daytime sleepiness were analysed using Partitioning Around Medoids clustering. The resulting phenotypes were characterised by pulmonary function, gas exchange, functional capacity, systemic biomarkers, and comorbidity burden. Longitudinal follow-up was available for 199 participants; survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, post-bronchodilator FEV1 and positive airway pressure (PAP) treatment. Five distinct sleep phenotypes were identified: preserved sleep physiology (good sleepers, 20.5%), curtailed sleep duration (short sleepers, 33%), altered sleep architecture with REM suppression (light sleepers, 18.5%), predominant nocturnal hypoxaemia (hypoxic sleepers, 20%), and severe sleep-disordered breathing (apnoeic sleepers, 8%). Despite similar airflow limitation and COPD symptom burden, phenotypes differed in gas exchange, functional capacity, systemic inflammation, and cardiometabolic comorbidities. During a median follow-up of 4.2 years, 56 participants (28.1%) died. Compared with good sleepers, hypoxic sleepers had a higher hazard of death after adjustment for age, sex, and FEV1 (HR 2.80, 95% CI 1.05-7.44). Following adjustment for PAP treatment, a higher mortality hazard was also observed among untreated apnoeic sleepers (HR 6.16, 95% CI 1.56-24.38). Multidimensional sleep phenotyping identified clinically distinct clusters of patients with COPD beyond conventional spirometric severity and apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI)-defined sleep-disordered breathing. These findings support sleep as a clinically relevant dimension of COPD heterogeneity, and warrant prospective validation of sleep-related traits and their clinical outcomes.
papers.journal: International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

papers.title: Peripheral GRM2 and GRM3 mRNA Alterations and Clinical Correlates in Insomnia Disorder: A Case-Control Pilot Study.
papers.abstract: This pilot study examined whether peripheral GRM2/GRM3 mRNA expression differed between chronic insomnia disorder (ID) and healthy controls (HCs) and correlated with emotional and polysomnographic (PSG) features. After PSG screening, 43 patients with chronic ID meeting DSM-5-TR criteria and 34 HCs with comparable age and sex distributions were included. Mood, sleep, and PSG parameters were assessed, and peripheral GRM2/GRM3 mRNA was quantified by RT-qPCR. Statistical analyses comprised group comparisons, age- and sex-adjusted regression, partial correlations with false discovery rate (FDR) correction, Bayesian analyses, sensitivity analyses, and exploratory receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. Compared with HCs, ID patients showed greater depressive and anxiety symptoms, poorer subjective sleep quality, and altered sleep architecture. Peripheral GRM2 and GRM3 mRNA expression was lower in ID patients, with both differences remaining significant after adjustment for age and sex (P=0.001; P=0.029). The apparent area under the curves (AUCs) were 0.744, 0.666, and 0.769 for GRM2, GRM3, and the combined model, respectively; corresponding cross-validated mean AUCs were 0.745, 0.645, and 0.732. Both GRM2 and GRM3 showed associations with emotional and sleep measures; the GRM3-PHQ-9 association remained significant after FDR correction (r=-0.373, P adj=0.020), while the GRM2-REM association showed Bayesian support (BF=4.473). These associations were attenuated after further adjustment for diagnostic group. Lower peripheral GRM2 and GRM3 expression was associated with chronic ID, with exploratory associations with selected emotional and sleep measures. These findings identify peripheral GRM2/GRM3 as candidate molecular correlates of ID. Independent external validation is required before clinical diagnostic application.

papers.title: Learning Out of Hours: A Narrative Review of Balancing Responsibility, Supervision, and Fatigue in Junior Doctor Training.
papers.abstract: Out-of-hours work is an integral component of postgraduate medical training and exposes junior doctors to clinical responsibility, uncertainty, competing demands, and acute deterioration in circumstances that may differ substantially from routine daytime practice. These conditions can provide valuable opportunities for experiential learning, but they can also reduce educational value when responsibility is accompanied by inadequate supervision, excessive workload or fatigue. This narrative review examines out-of-hours work as a learning environment for junior doctors, integrating literature on workplace learning, autonomy and supervision, prioritisation and decision-making, deterioration and escalation, handover and teamwork, sleep disruption and fatigue, and educational interventions designed to prepare trainees for out-of-hours practice. The literature suggests that the educational value of out-of-hours work arises not from independence alone, but from meaningful clinical responsibility within an appropriately supported environment. Responsibility can provide opportunities for autonomous initial assessment, prioritisation, and decision-making under uncertainty, while the recognition of personal limits and appropriate escalation are themselves components of developing clinical judgement. Simulation and structured preparation may help trainees rehearse these demands before substantial clinical responsibility is assumed, while feedback, reflection, and review of subsequent patient outcomes can help convert clinical exposure into learning. However, excessive workload, inadequate supervision, and fatigue may impair both the opportunity and the capacity to learn. Out-of-hours training should therefore aim to preserve authentic responsibility while ensuring that autonomy is graded to capability, senior support remains accessible, workload is manageable, and opportunities for feedback and recovery are maintained. We propose that effective out-of-hours learning occurs within a zone of meaningful responsibility in which trainees are sufficiently challenged to develop clinical judgement without becoming unsupported or physiologically unsustainable. Designing this environment requires attention not only to individual preparedness but also to supervision, staffing, workload, handover, feedback, and rota design.

papers.title: The role of histamine in narcolepsy type 1: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Narcolepsy type 1 (NT1) is a chronic neurological disorder characterized mainly by impaired wakefulness maintenance and dysregulated rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which markedly affects patients' daytime functioning and quality of life. The core pathological basis of NT1 is the selective loss of orexinergic neurons. The orexinergic system regulates histaminergic neurons in the tuberomammillary nucleus (TMN) through anatomical projections and functional excitation, while the histaminergic system contributes to cortical activation, arousal maintenance, and attention regulation. Therefore, the orexinergic and histaminergic systems can be regarded as interconnected and functionally complementary components of the arousal network. Previous studies have suggested alterations in histaminergic signaling in NT1, although the specific mechanisms underlying its role in NT1 remain incompletely understood. Current evidence suggests that histamine may play a modulatory role in NT1-associated phenotypes. This review summarizes the physiological functions of the histaminergic system in arousal regulation and discusses its interaction with the orexinergic system. It further analyzes the role of HA in NT1, its influence on clinical phenotypes, and related therapeutic strategies, with the aim of providing insights for mechanistic research and precision treatment of NT1.

papers.title: Auditory sustained potential as a biomarker of language functioning in children with autism and its implication in clinical trials.
papers.abstract: Most children with autism have language impairment, however, its neural mechanisms are not well understood. A potential biomarker associated with language in autism is a 40Hz Auditory Steady-State Response (ASSR) triggered by periodic click-trains which in electroencephalogram (EEG) evokes two types of responses - 40Hz steady-state gamma response (ASSR) and sustained potential (SP). Although these responses represent low-level auditory processing, they correspond to different stages of sound perception/analysis and are essential in processing of spectrally/temporally complex sounds. However, until now there were no studies focusing on the potentials of these responses in clinical trials. The present open-label pilot study evaluated the effects of the probiotic beverage supplement Bio-K+ in children with autism (N = 19). Participants were assessed at three timepoints: T0 (baseline), T14 (14 weeks after intervention), and T22 (8 weeks after intervention, post-supplementation follow-up assessment), including EEG 40Hz ASSR and behavioral phenotyping. First, at T0 we showed a reduction of SP amplitude in children with autism compared to controls, and this reduction was associated with lower speech/language/communication scores. Second, the amplitude of SP became significantly more negative during the probiotic supplementation period and, by T14, was no longer significantly different from the observed in TD controls. Finally, these changes in the amplitude of SP were associated with improvement in speech/language/communication scores. This study showed that the SP as well as its change was related specifically to speech/language/communication but not to other behavioral measures and has a potential to be used in future clinical trials.

papers.title: N-back electroencephalography asymmetry and peripheral immune cell subpopulation composition.
papers.abstract: Cognitive deficits such as working memory impairment and peripheral inflammation frequently occur together in neuropsychiatric conditions, yet the relationship between them remains poorly understood. To address this gap, the present study examines these associations in healthy young adults to establish baseline relationships between peripheral immune cell subpopulations and neural activity without clinical confounds. The aim of this study is to investigate whether the relative proportions of peripheral immune cell subpopulations are associated with EEG asymmetry during a working memory task and with task performance. EEG data were recorded from 24 healthy participants during a 2-back working memory task. Relative EEG asymmetry indices were computed for four frequency bands: alpha, beta, delta, and theta. 2-back task performance was also calculated. Peripheral blood was collected for DNA extraction and genome-wide DNA methylation analysis to estimate the relative proportions of immune cell subpopulations. Estimated proportions were Center Log-Ratio-transformed. Spearman's correlation and multiple linear regression were used to identify associations between EEG asymmetry, relative immune markers, and n-back task performance. Our analysis revealed that theta asymmetry was associated with CLR-transformed proportions of natural killer cells (p=0.035) and CD4+ T cells (p = 0.027). 2-back task target accuracy was nearly correlated with granulocytes (p = 0.082) and CD8+ T cell proportions (p=0.016); however, these associations did not remain significant after Bonferroni correction. Despite this, both immune markers significantly predicted 2-back target accuracy across three multiple linear regression models (model 1: p = 0.005, model 2: p = 0.002, model 3: p = 0.002).

papers.title: Bridging language phenotypes, neural dynamics and gene regulation in autism.
papers.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASDs) affect approximately 1% of the global population, with prevalence rising over recent decades. Although ASDs are heritable (~70%), translating genetic findings into effective therapeutics remains challenging due to the vast number of implicated risk genes (>700) and the limited influence of individual genes on disease expression. Their collective impact and convergent expression patterns of small-effect genes provide insights into ASD-related neurobiological mechanisms. Current interventions remain symptom-focused and do not address underlying neurodevelopmental mechanisms. Emerging approaches in functional genomics offer new insights into ASD pathogenesis by exploring gene expression diversity, yet clinical applications remain distant. Language deficits are among the most frequent and disabling features of ASD, profoundly affecting individuals' and families' quality of life. Recent evidence from neuroimaging and electrophysiology studies suggests disrupted neural oscillatory dynamics are linked to language deficits in ASD. Several ASD-associated genes have been implicated in biological pathways involved in the regulation of brain oscillatory dynamics, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between genetic variation, altered brain rhythms, and language impairment. We propose a neurophysiological imaging genetics framework that leverages neural oscillatory profiles as endophenotypes for targeted investigation and as functional readouts of gene expression. Within this framework, neuromodulation is proposed as an experimental approach to investigate and potentially modulate altered oscillatory dynamics associated with speech communication deficits in ASD, while integrating oscillation-related ASD candidate genes into a symptom-oriented model of functional genomics. This approach shows how integrating genetic variation, non-invasive neuroimaging, and behavioral phenotypes can advance our understanding of ASD and inform targeted, mechanism-based interventions.

papers.title: Inter-subject correlations and their behavioral associations vary across movies: Implications for generalizability.
papers.abstract: Movie-watching functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has become increasingly popular in neuroscience. Movie-fMRI data are commonly analyzed using inter-subject correlation (ISC), which quantifies the similarity of neural time series across individuals. Differences in ISC during movie viewing have been associated with psychological traits and clinical diagnoses. However, most studies investigating group differences in ISC or ISC-behavior associations have drawn conclusions from a single movie. Because ISC is inherently stimulus driven, effects observed for one movie may not generalize to another. Yet, the extent to which ISC patterns and ISC-behavior associations depend on the specific movie being viewed has received limited systematic attention. Here, we analyzed three independent datasets comprising 318 subjects and 36 movies in total to quantify between-movie variability in ISC and assess its consequences for ISC-behavior associations. Across datasets, ISC varied between movies throughout the cortex. This variability was spatially heterogeneous: regions with stronger ISC showed greater between-movie variability. Movie-specific inter-subject representational similarity analysis revealed distinct spatial distributions of ISC-behavior associations, with little overlap between movies. This pattern was observed for two distinct behavioral constructs. These findings suggest that ISC-behavior associations can be strongly movie specific.

papers.title: Rotigotine transdermal patch in Parkinson's disease: a narrative review of pharmacology, clinical evidence, special-population management, and health economics.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) requires lifelong dopaminergic therapy, yet oral routes are frequently compromised by gastrointestinal dysfunction, dysphagia, and perioperative fasting. Abrupt withdrawal of oral dopaminergic drugs may precipitate severe motor deterioration or parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome. Rotigotine transdermal patch delivers 24-h continuous dopaminergic stimulation (CDS) via a non-ergot dopamine agonist (DA) formulation that bypasses first-pass metabolism and gastrointestinal absorption, and may be particularly useful when oral dopaminergic delivery becomes unreliable or is not possible. To synthesize published evidence on rotigotine pharmacology, clinical efficacy, management in vulnerable populations, safety, real-world effectiveness, and health economics, with emphasis on the incremental contribution of a scenario-based, Asia/China-inclusive, and pharmacy-oriented narrative relative to prior general reviews. Narrative review of randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, regulatory documents, pharmacoeconomic models, and prospective observational studies identified through structured literature search and bibliographic screening. Transdermal bioavailability is approximately 37% versus less than 5% for oral rotigotine. Pivotal Chinese trials SP0914 (early PD: UPDRS II + III -4.9 vs. -0.2) and SP1037 (advanced PD: placebo-adjusted off-time reduction -1.20 h/d [95% CI -1.83 to -0.57]; within-group change -2.36 h/d) demonstrated efficacy; meta-analyses support motor and selected non-motor benefits, including sleep, mood, and gastrointestinal tolerability, whereas swallowing-related signals remain preliminary and based mainly on small observational studies. Perioperative fasting, dysphagia, end-stage disease, and hepatorenal impairment represent clinically important scenarios in which non-oral delivery may be considered, although supporting evidence outside pivotal motor trials is often limited. Application-site reactions (ASRs) are the principal local adverse events; structured 14-day site rotation reduced ASR from 50.0% to 20.3% (P = 0.0373). Chinese cost-effectiveness analyses reported an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of 1,118,617.81 CNY per quality-adjusted life year versus pramipexole immediate-release at market price, with price-sensitivity thresholds of 28.5% and 9.5% reductions. Rotigotine provides CDS for patients with PD when oral delivery is unreliable; individualized patient selection, structured pharmaceutical care, and updated pharmacoeconomic evaluation are warranted.

papers.title: Psychedelics and Reward Processing: Before and After the 1970 Controlled Substances Act.
papers.abstract: This narrative review traces how the scientific understanding of psychedelics has intersected with "reward processing" from before the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) era to the present, emphasizing how cultural and regulatory climates shaped what was viewed as an acceptable research question. Reward processing is treated as a family of partially overlapping phenomena: (1) reward-linked behavior (e.g., self-administration, conditioned place preference, reinstatement), (2) reward-circuit signals (e.g., mesolimbic dopamine dynamics, electrophysiology, human electroencephalography potentials), and (3) clinically relevant outcomes in substance use disorder (SUD) (e.g., withdrawal severity, consumption, relapse). Across these measures, the literature repeatedly adopts two framing logics: "liability framing," which prioritizes misuse potential and dependence risk, and "therapeutic framing," which treats psychedelics as tools for probing and potentially reconfiguring reward circuitry and learning. Organized by decade, the review shows that the 1960s already contained both motifs, with adjunctive therapeutic hopes alongside early reinforcement assays, while the CSA era increasingly systematized a hazard-first posture that defined the late 1970s through the 2000s, referred to as the "psychedelic dark age." Within those constraints, monoamine and receptor pharmacology (including serotonin-dopamine interactions) became a dominant tool for investigating reward, and ibogaine programs loudly reintroduced a therapeutically oriented anti-addiction narrative. In the 2000s, serotonergic control of dopaminergic reward systems and entactogen models, including social reward, broadened the mechanistic frame. In the 2010s and 2020s, the field's momentum shifted toward therapeutic models, circuit plasticity, computationally interpretable reward signals, and renewed clinical work in SUD. The review argues that a central bottleneck is not a lack of provocative acute findings but rather a lack of experimental programs that bridge behavior, circuit signals, and longitudinal clinical endpoints. We therefore propose that revisiting important concepts and findings discussed herein with recently developed technology and approaches (e.g., cue-evoked signals, learning parameters, photometry) across dose, time, and sex would advance the field. We highlight practical study shifts to move toward an integrated account of how psychedelics modulate reward-relevant brain activity and behavior.

papers.title: Dorsal Raphe Revisited: A Systems Neuroscience Lens on Psychedelic Drug Action.
papers.abstract: Psychedelics rose to prominence in the 1960s, around the same time when neurobiologists identified the midbrain raphe as the brain's primary source of serotonin. It is therefore no surprise that early studies on classical psychedelics like d-lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) focused on their effects within this brainstem nucleus. This review traces the arc of discovery: from the initial report in 1968 that LSD suppresses the firing of serotonergic neurons in the rat midbrain raphe, through more than 15 years of intensive work dissecting the pharmacology and receptor mechanisms. Early hypotheses erroneously suggested the serotonergic neurons as potential drivers of the acute hallucinogenic effects, but the conceptual framework gradually shifted after relating neural activity to behavior. We conclude this brief commentary by revisiting these early findings in light of current knowledge of the serotonergic circuits. Collectively, the pioneering studies laid the foundation for thinking about how psychedelics act on the brain through the lens of neurophysiology.

papers.title: Outcomes and Complications of Monobloc Versus Le Fort III Procedures for Treating Craniosynostosis: A Literature Review.
papers.abstract: Craniosynostosis is a congenital disorder resulting in the early fusion of several bones in the skull, causing a deformity of the head and facial structures. The 2 most commonly performed surgical procedures to treat craniosynostosis include the monobloc and Le Fort III procedures. This literature review compares the functional and anatomical outcomes and complications between the monobloc and Le Fort III procedures for treating craniosynostosis. A PubMed search was conducted to identify studies assessing the outcomes following monobloc and Le Fort procedures. Data on anatomical changes, ophthalmic, airway, and neurological sequelae, as well as miscellaneous infectious or aesthetic complications were extracted from each study. A total of 63 articles were included for analysis. The average length of midface advancement across distraction and nondistraction procedures was significantly higher in the monobloc cases (14.28 mm; 98.8% of patients with distraction) compared with Le Fort III cases (12.26 mm; 63% of patients with distraction) (P = 0.002). Both procedures exhibited similar rates of obstructive sleep apnea improvement. Cerebrospinal fluid leakage (69 of 373 monobloc patients; 15 of 448 Le Fort III patients) (P ≤ 0.001), seizures (8 of 373 monobloc surgery patients), and meningitis (9 of 373 and 2 of 448, monobloc and Le Fort III patients respectively) (P = 0.01) were observed. In summary, this review demonstrates that both the monobloc and Le Fort III procedures are effective in producing maxillofacial advancement and correcting craniosynostosis, with the monobloc procedure demonstrating significantly greater average advancement. Future research should investigate the comparison of aesthetic and obstructive sleep apnea outcomes further.
